title: APEX Collapses Streaming Video DMD Into One Shared Network
summary: Tsinghua and NVIDIA's APEX paper shares one network between generator and fake estimator, cutting GPU memory 4.5 GiB and iteration time 3.3 seconds.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- APEX merges generator and fake estimator into one network using shifted text conditions, cutting GPU memory from 102.7 to 98.2 GiB.
- Iteration time drops from 35.9 to 32.6 seconds per GPU by sharing parameters across generation and fake velocity estimation passes.
- Human study shows 30 percent net preference on instruction following but 8.6 percent penalty on motion quality versus baseline DMD training.


Tsinghua and NVIDIA have released a new streaming-video architecture that collapses Distribution Matching Distillation's two-network setup into one shared model. APEX uses a shifted text condition to estimate fake velocity inside the generator itself, eliminating the separate fake-score network and cutting peak GPU memory from 102.7 to 98.2 GiB per GPU. The paper, published on Hugging Face on November 11, 2026, demonstrates that parameter sharing between generation and estimation passes drops mean iteration time from 35.9 to 32.6 seconds during training.


## How the Shared Network Works


The original Distribution Matching Distillation approach trains two separate networks: one for generation and one for scoring fake samples. APEX merges both functions into a single model by routing different text conditions to different roles. The abstract explains that "the original text condition selects generation, while a shifted condition selects fake estimation using the same parameters." A negated text condition tells the generator to estimate its own fake velocity, sharing all parameters with the forward generation pass. This design removes the need for a second network entirely, delivering the 4.5 GiB memory saving and 3.3-second speedup per iteration.


## Benchmark Results on StreamAV-Bench


On the 320-case StreamAV-Bench, APEX scores 3.856 on video instruction fulfillment in the Progressive track, edging S2-Avatar's 3.831. Visual aesthetics reach 0.641898 across both tracks, compared to 0.632606 for the baseline. The instruction-fulfillment gain is modest but consistent across the test set. The paper does not publish an ablation isolating which component of the shared-network setup drives the visual-aesthetics improvement, leaving open the question of whether condition shifting or parameter reuse is the primary factor.


## Human Study Shows Instruction-Following Gains


A 70-pair human study on 180-second image-to-video sequences gives APEX a net 30 percent preference on instruction following, with 22 wins, 47 ties, and 1 loss. However, motion quality shows an 8.6 percent penalty versus the DMD baseline. The paper reports that "human raters favor APEX most strongly on instruction following, with +30.0% net preference," but does not explain why motion quality declines. The absence of an ablation study leaves unclear whether the shared-network design inherently trades motion fidelity for instruction adherence, or whether hyperparameter tuning could close the gap.


## Officially Released on November 11, 2026


Tsinghua and NVIDIA published the APEX paper on Hugging Face today. The abstract extends the architecture to streaming video using condition shifting, a technique that routes the same parameter set to two distinct estimation tasks. The release adds one more data point to the 64 AI video stories tracked in the last 90 days, underscoring the pace of optimization research in video generation. No code repository or pre-trained checkpoint has been announced alongside the paper.


## What This Means


APEX demonstrates that streaming-video models can collapse multi-network training pipelines into a single shared architecture without sacrificing instruction-following accuracy. The 4.5 GiB memory reduction and 3.3-second iteration speedup open the door to longer training runs on the same hardware budget, potentially improving model quality at fixed cost. However, the 8.6 percent motion-quality penalty suggests that parameter sharing introduces subtle trade-offs that future work will need to address. Organizations building streaming-video applications should monitor whether follow-up releases isolate the motion-quality regression and offer tuning strategies to recover baseline performance.
